title: A 4.1-Billion-Year-Old Rock From Mars: Teghaza 001 Is Among the Oldest Martian Meteorites Ever Found
excerpt: NASA-funded scientists have dated the 800-gram meteorite Teghaza 001 to about 4.1 billion years, making it one of the oldest pieces of Mars ever found on Earth.
content:
A rose-colored rock found on a salt plain in Mali in 2022 has turned out to be one of the oldest pieces of Mars ever found on Earth — a meteorite about 4.1 billion years old that carries a record of how the planet’s crust formed and how water later changed it.

The meteorite, named Teghaza 001 after the salt plain where it was discovered, weighs about 800 grams (nearly 2 pounds). It was originally believed to be a shergottite, the most common form of Martian meteorite, but closer study showed it is far older: roughly the same age as the previous record-holder, ALH84001, and about two billion years older than the next-oldest contender, known as Black Beauty.

Two separate teams of NASA-funded scientists studied the rock. One team examined its water content and published its findings in the journal Science Advances in June 2026. The second team, led by Yang Liu of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory and Lee Saper of NASA’s Ames Research Center, published its results on October 29, 2026, in the journal Science.

Unlike ALH84001, which is composed of a single mineral, Teghaza 001 contains a variety of igneous materials. That mix — especially its zircon crystals — let the scientists match its mineral balance to Mars’ southern highlands and narrow its origin to a small set of candidate locations there. The researchers said the rock “tells a story about how the planet’s crust formed from cooling magma before it was eventually altered by subsurface water,” with that water alteration dated to around 4.1 billion years ago.

The dating trick that preserved the rock

The team also pioneered a gentler way to date it. Rather than dissolving and analyzing the entire sample, Caltech researcher Francois Tissot used a technique called in-situ rubidium-strontium dating, analyzing single mineral grains on a piece smaller than a fingernail. That leaves the bulk of the meteorite untouched for future researchers.

“Right now, we are one of very few labs in the world able to perform this kind of age-dating, and the first to date such an ancient Martian meteorite,” Tissot said. “Our hope is to pave the way for dating even more Martian meteorites, or samples returned from other planets, their moons and asteroids.”

For Webb County readers, the find is a reminder of how much of Mars’ earliest history arrives here unannounced: a rock knocked off the planet billions of years ago, carried across the solar system, and read — grain by grain — in a laboratory on Earth.
